list.listitem: Screen high-risk infants (preterm or small-for-gestational age, started on cow's milk before age 1 year, or consuming greater than 24 ounces of milk per day) for iron-deficiency anemia. B
Serum ferritin is the best test for iron-deficiency anemia. If serum ferritin is low, total iron-binding capacity and serum iron tests add little information. B

Screen all pregnant women for iron-deficiency anemia and consider giving prophylactic oral iron supplements (30 mg/day). C There is inconclusive evidence, however, that routine prenatal iron supplementation improves maternal or infant clinical health outcomes.
Consider ordering serum folate, vitamin B12, serum ferritin, and reticulocyte count when anemia is noted to streamline the diagnostic evaluation. C

Patients older than 50 years, younger patients with a positive family history or risk factors for cancer, and older patients with anemia and serum ferritin levels less than 100 mg/dL should be evaluated for colon cancer. B

background.definition: Anemia is a decrease in the serum hemoglobin or hematocrit level caused by decreased red blood cell (RBC) production, increased RBC destruction, or blood loss.

list.listitem: In the United States, iron-deficiency anemia is most common in young children (5.7%), teenage girls (5.9%), young women (5.8%), and elderly men (4.4%). Canada and northern Europe have similar rates. Around the world, anemia has a higher prevalence because of nutritional deficiencies (eg, lack of dietary meat), malaria, intestinal parasites, and genetic factors.
In the United States, pernicious anemia occurs in approximately 2.7% of women and 1.4% of men older than 60 years; the prevalence is 4.3% in black women and 4.0% in white women.

In a review of original research from 13 countries (Australia, Brazil, Canada, Guatemala, India, Kenya, Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, Sri Lanka, Tanzania, the United States, and Venezuela), higher rates of anemia were found among indigenous populations. For example, in an Australian study, the rate of anemia among Aboriginal children was 16.4% vs. 4.2% among non-Aboriginal children. In the US, the prevalence of anemia among Alaskan Native vs. non-Native Alaskan children ages 24 to 59 months was 22% vs. 12%.
Moderate to severe anemia is associated with small-for-gestational-age outcomes (odds ratio [OR] 1.53; 95% CI, 1.24-1.87).

Preoperative anemia is associated with poor post-surgical outcomes such as increased mortality (OR 2.9; 95% CI, 2.30-3.68), acute kidney injury (OR 3.75; 95% CI, 2.95-4.76) and infection (OR 1.93; 95% CI, 1.17-3.18). The studies were quite heterogeneous, however, and it is not known if anemia is an independent risk factor for poor outcomes or a marker of underlying chronic disease.

In a retrospective study of 620 patients with upper tract urothelial carcinoma, investigators found that patients with preoperative anemia had worse overall survival (hazard ratio [HR] 1.76; 95% CI, 1.35-2.28), cancer-specific survival (HR 1.72; 95% CI, 1.28-2.30), and disease recurrence-free survival (HR 1.43; 95% CI, 1.11-1.83).

In the ICU setting, lower hemoglobin was associated with a higher probability of worsening respiratory dysfunction scores the following day, but there was no association with brain dysfunction, renal dysfunction, or ICU mortality.

For patients with coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19), authors of a meta-analysis of 23 articles including 573,928 patients found an association between anemia and an elevated risk of COVID-19 mortality (pooled effect size 1.47, 95% CI 1.30-1.67).

Authors of a meta-analysis of 18 studies found an association between iron-deficiency anemia and celiac disease, which was present in 4.8%. Approximately 1 in 31 patients with iron-deficiency anemia had histologic evidence of celiac disease.
See Differential Diagnosis table for common causes of anemia.
Repeated blood tests in hospitalized patients can be a cause of anemia.

The bone marrow produces RBCs, which have an average life span of approximately 120 days. Anemia can be caused by each of the following 3 mechanisms (or a combination of 2 or 3): Decreased RBC production, due to lack of or reduced use of key nutrients, bone marrow suppression or disorders, or decreased RBC production-stimulating hormones. Increased RBC destruction (as in inherited and acquired hemolytic anemias). Acute blood loss (eg, gastrointestinal bleeding) or chronic blood loss (eg, menorrhagia).
The presence of inflammation can mask the presence of iron-deficiency anemia.

Systemic inflammation can decrease erythrocyte production and survival. This type of anemia can be a main or contributing factor in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), chronic heart failure, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and cystic fibrosis. Preservation of iron stores distinguishes it from iron deficiency anemia.

Iron homeostasis is maintained by interaction between hepcidin, an iron-regulatory hormone produced by hepatocytes, and ferroportin, a transmembrane protein and hepcidin receptor that transfers iron from cells to plasma. Hepcidin synthesis decreases when iron levels are low and increases when iron is abundant and during states of inflammation.

If screening pregnant women for iron-deficiency anemia, screen at their first visit. Although iron supplementation improves maternal hematologic indices, the United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF, 2015) found inconclusive evidence that routine prenatal iron supplementation improves maternal or infant clinical health outcomes and therefor gave screening for iron-deficiency anemia an I rating (insufficient evidence). This recommendation addresses screening and supplementation in pregnant women and adolescents living in the United States who do not have symptoms of iron deficiency anemia (IDA). It does not address pregnant women who are malnourished, have symptoms of iron deficiency anemia, or have special hematologic conditions or nutritional needs.

The USPSTF (2015) also found insufficient evidence for or against screening for iron-deficiency anemia in asymptomatic children aged 6 to 12 months. The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) recommends universal screening at 12 months with hemoglobin concentration and risk factor assessment. Selective screening can be performed at any age when risk factors for iron deficiency and IDA have been identified. If the Hb level is less than 11.0 mg/dL at 12 months of age, then further evaluation for IDA is required to establish it as a cause of anemia. Authors of a systematic review found, similar to pregnant women, that iron supplementation for iron-deficiency anemia in young children improves hematologic values, but there is insufficient evidence that supplementation improves clinical outcomes.

For newborn screening, use of a hematology analyzer is the gold standard for measuring hemoglobin concentration and outperforms blood gas analyzer and HemoCue®, using either venous or capillary blood samples.

Serum reticulocyte hemoglobin is more accurate than serum hemoglobin levels as a screening tool for IDA for toddlers. However, this is not currently available in most ambulatory settings so screening recommendations have not changed.
Reticulocyte hemoglobin content is also a good marker of IDA in preterm infants at 3 to 4 months corrected age, and may be superior to ferritin, MCV and transferrin saturation.
Repeat hemoglobin testing within 24 hours for hospitalized patients is of limited value; there is no significant change in almost 90% of patients, especially when continued bleeding is not suspected.

Obtain a family and genetic history from all patients, especially those of Mediterranean, African, Middle Eastern, East Indian, Hispanic, or Asian ancestry who may become parents to identify those at greater risk for hemoglobinopathies. Screening for hemoglobin variants should be performed at the first prenatal visit for all pregnant women known to be from racial and ethnic groups at risk.

Begin low-dose iron (30 mg/day) oral supplementation for pregnant women, starting from the first prenatal visit. However, routine iron supplementation for nonanemic pregnant women is of uncertain benefit. The UK guidelines do not recommend routine iron supplementation for all women during pregnancy.
American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG, 2021) recommend low-dose iron supplementation starting in the first trimester to decrease the prevalence of maternal anemia at delivery.

Authors of a randomized clinical trial of 400 newborns found that delayed cord clamping (at least 180 seconds after birth) vs. immediate cord clamping (<10 seconds after birth) increased infant iron stores at 4 months of age although there was no difference in the prevalence of infant anemia. Assessment of outcomes at later ages is needed. In one RCT of 204 newborns, milking the cord was comparable to delayed clamping on neonatal outcomes.

Consider routine iron supplementation for asymptomatic children aged 6 to 12 months who are at increased risk for IDA. Supplementation is of no benefit in healthy, full-term infants who are not at risk for anemia.

The AAP, by consensus, recommend supplementation of exclusively breast-fed infants older than 4 months and partially breastfed infants (more than half of their daily feedings as human milk) with 1 mg/kg per day or oral iron until iron-rich foods such as iron-fortified cereals are introduced into the diet.

Iron supplementation with a multivitamin including 10 to 11 mg of elemental iron in a group of high-risk infants did not prevent iron-deficiency anemia,so give iron-enriched formula and cereals, as well as ferrous sulfate 1 to 2 mg/kg per day, up to 15 mg total per day.

The provision of micronutrient powder containing at least iron, zinc and vitamin A vs. placebo to children in low income countries in Asia, Africa and the Caribbean reduced anemia by 31% (six trials, RR 0.69; 95% CI, 0.60-0.78, 11 low-quality studies) and iron deficiency by 51% (four trials, RR 0.49; 95% CI, 0.35-0.67) in children 6 to 23 months of age. The benefit of this strategy on survival is unclear.

The use of intermittent iron supplements (one, two or three times weekly on non-consecutive days) was effective in reducing the risk of anemia in menstruating women over placebo (RR 0.65; 95% CI, 0.49-0.87) and appears to be as effective as daily supplementation (RR 1.09; 95% CI, 0.93-1.29). Similarly, use of intermittent iron supplements was effective in reducing the risk of anemia in children under age 12 years over placebo (RR 0.51; 95% CI, 0.37-0.72) but was not as effective as daily supplementation (RR 1.23; 95% CI, 1.04-1.47).
Administration of erythropoietin at 8 or more days of age in preterm infants reduces the use of one or more RBC transfusions (NNT = 6) but not the total volume (mL/kg) of RBCs transfused per infant.

list.listitem: The World Health Organization definitions of anemia are serum hemoglobin below 13 g/dL for adult men and below 12 g/dL for adult women.
Modified proposed criteria based on age, race, and sex are shown in .

In patients with anemia, the American Gastroenterological Association (AGA, 2020) recommends using a cutoff of 45 ng/mL when using ferritin to diagnose iron deficiency. In patients with inflammatory conditions or CKD, other laboratory tests such as C-reactive protein, transferrin saturation, or soluble transferring saturation may be needed in conjunction with ferritin to diagnose iron deficiency anemia.

In asymptomatic postmenopausal women and men with IDA, the AGA (2020) recommends bidirectional endoscopy over no endoscopy. This recommendation assumes there is no other unequivocal explanation for iron deficiency anemia, particularly in young men, after a thorough history and physical examination.
Clinical presentation depends on degree and rate of anemia development. Think acute blood loss with hypovolemia and associated symptoms of orthostasis, fatigue, and thirst.

Chronic anemia will manifest when oxygen demand exceeds oxygen delivery to cells, and timing will differ according to patient baseline status (young and healthy versus old patient with heart disease). Although most symptoms and signs are nonspecific, primary complaints include fatigue, dyspnea with exertion or at rest, and palpitations.
More severe anemia will cause lethargy and confusion and may lead to life-threatening cardiac complications, especially in patients with advanced atherosclerosis.

Key elements of the history include: time course of anemia (acute, subacute, chronic); ethnicity and family history of anemia; medication use (eg, NSAIDs); dietary intake of iron and leafy greens; environmental/workplace exposures (eg, lead, benzene), and any comorbidities.

Key physical signs of anemia include: heart murmur; signs of malignancy auch as lymphadenopathy, night sweats, and weight loss; skin survey for bruising or other evidence of coagulopathy; and the presence of pallor and jaundice (hemolysis, liver disease).

Conjunctival pallor is helpful when present (positive likelihood ratio [LR] = 4.5), but its absence does not rule out anemia (negative LR = 0.6). The sensitivity and specificity of the overall clinical impression is only approximately 70% for the diagnosis of anemia.
Order a complete blood count including indices, white count differential, and platelets. MCV is the first key point in the diagnostic algorithm.

Order reticulocyte count, which can be corrected according to anemia severity with the reticulocyte production index (RPI) to assess bone marrow response. A normal RPI is 1, and an adequate bone marrow response to anemia is 2 or more (see ).
The reticulocyte hemoglobin content is a better indicator of iron deficiency in infants than hemoglobin.
Obtain a peripheral blood smear for morphology changes when anemia etiology is unclear.

Serum ferritin is the most accurate test for IDA and anemia of chronic disease. A serum ferritin cutoff of <15 μg/L is a specific but not sensitive cutoff for IDA based on limited data. Serum iron and total iron-binding capacity (transferrin saturation) are less accurate and are not needed unless the diagnosis remains in doubt.

In patients who are pregnant, elderly, or who have low WBC, vitamin B12 levels may be spuriously low. For patients with indeterminate vitamin B12 levels (100-400 mcg/dL), serum methylmalonic acid level (MMA) is recommended to confirm B12 deficiency.
High serum homocysteine aids in the diagnosis of folate deficiency since recent dietary changes may affect serum folate levels.

Order indirect bilirubin (elevated with hemolysis), LDH (elevated with hemolysis), and haptoglobin (low with hemolysis) when hemolysis is suspected. None of these studies indicate the reason for the hemolysis, only its presence. If warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia is suspected, a positive direct antiglobulin test (Coombs’ test) is seen in 95%. In cold agglutinin disease, the Coombs’ test is typically negative for IgG but positive for C3 fragments and a high titer of cold agglutinins (titer of >1:128) may be found along with antibody specificity to I or i red-cell antigens.
Hemoglobin electrophoresis is recommended for diagnosis of beta-thalassemia and sickle cell anemia; for alpha-thalassemia, a genetic test may be needed.

A point-of-care test, the Sickle SCAN™ can be performed in individuals >1 year of age using capillary blood. In one study with 71 subjects, the test was 99% sensitive and 99% specific for the diagnosis of HbSS, HbAS, HbSC, HbAC, and HbAA.
Flow cytometry is a highly sensitive and specific screening test for hereditary spherocytosis (LR+ 107, LR− 0.036).

The Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine recommends use of middle cerebral artery (MCA) peak systolic velocity measured by ultrasound Doppler interrogation to detect fetal anemia for women who are at risk of having an anemic fetus. If a fetus is deemed at significant risk for severe fetal anemia (MCA greater than 1.5 multiples of the median or hydropic), fetal blood sampling should be performed in a referral center with expertise in invasive fetal therapy to prepare for an intrauterine transfusion, unless the pregnancy is at a gestational age when the risks associated with delivery are considered to be less than those associated with the procedure.
Bone marrow examination should be considered for elderly patients with mild anemia but only if results will change the treatment plan.
See for an algorithmic approach to diagnosis.
Elderly patients with IDA are at significantly increased risk of gastrointestinal malignancy (RR = 31) and an endoscopic work up is recommended.

Patients with anemia and a serum ferritin level of less than 100 ng/mL have a significantly increased risk for a malignant or highly dysplastic gastrointestinal polyp and should undergo a colonoscopy.
Patients with IDA and no source of bleeding found on an initial gastrointestinal evaluation need further evaluation if their anemia does not respond to iron replacement.

cell.label: Patient with anemia (hemoglobin <13 g/dL for men, <12 g/dL for women). Review indices, perform careful history and physical. Evidence of bleeding, or premenopausal woman?
MCV >95 or symptoms consistent with B12 or folate deficiency?
Low MCV and at risk for thallessemia?
Order peripheral smear for megalocytes, B12 (if not already ordered), serum creatinine, ALT or GGT, TSH, Epo levels, and bone marrow biopsy. Anemia of chronic disease likely.
Iron-deficiency anemia. Treat source and provide iron replacement, follow-up serum ferritin and hemoglobin in 1-2 months. Colonoscopy if older than 40-50 years or red flags for cancer.
Order hemoglobin electrophoresis. Diagnostic for thallessemia?
Thallessemia. Order serum ferritin to rule out co-existing IDA due to chronic blood loss.
Order serum methylmalonic acid and homocysteine.
Serum ferritin and appropriate investigation to identify source. Serum ferritin low and likely source identified?
